A.explanation: Gives $25 \text{MHz}$, far too small because it treats $6.0 \text{ cm}$ as much larger than half a wavelength.

B.explanation: Gives $50 \text{MHz}$, far too small because it mistakes the $6.0 \text{ cm}$ antinode separation for a full wavelength calculation error.

C.explanation: Uses $\lambda = 2 \times 6.0 \text{ cm} = 0.12 \text{ m}$ and $f = v/\lambda = 2.5 \times 10^9 \text{ Hz}$.

D.explanation: Gives $5.0 \text{ GHz}$, twice the correct value because it treats the $6.0 \text{ cm}$ antinode separation as one full wavelength.

hints: Notice the two melted spots are both antinodes and are $6.0 \text{ cm}$ apart along the chocolate bar.
Recall the stationary wave rule for the distance between two adjacent antinodes in terms of wavelength $\lambda$.
Combine the wavelength from the $6.0 \text{ cm}$ spacing with $v = f\lambda$ using $v = 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough: Identify the useful data: melted spots mark positions of maximum microwave heating, so they are adjacent antinodes separated by $6.0 \text{ cm} = 0.060 \text{ m}$.
State the stationary wave rule: adjacent antinode to adjacent antinode is half a wavelength, so $0.060 = \lambda/2$.
Use the wave equation $v = f\lambda$ rearranged to $f = v/\lambda$ with $v = 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Substitute: $f = (3.0 \times 10^8)/(0.12) = 2.5 \times 10^9 \text{ Hz} = 2.5 \text{ GHz}$. This is option C.
